title: Screening and identification of a novel umami peptide with in vitro anti-inflammatory potential from sea cucumber protein: Integration of flavoromics, bioinformatic prediction, molecular simulation and experimental validation.
authors: Chu, Zhongxing; Long, Can; Xu, Kangjie; Zhang, Xingjing; Qin, Dandan; Hu, Zuomin; Zhou, Yaping; Luo, Feijun; Lin, Qinlu
abstract: Sea cucumber protein was sequentially hydrolyzed with pepsin, trypsin, and enterokinase to obtain peptides with desirable taste characteristics and immunomodulatory potential. Multi-scale characterization, flavoromics, peptidomics, bioinformatic screening, molecular simulations, and cellular assays were employed to investigate the structural changes, flavor remodeling, and bioactivity of the resulting hydrolysates. Results showed that hydrolysis disrupted the compact protein structure, induced conformational unfolding, and yielded short peptides (0.5-1.5 kDa) with enhanced hydrophilicity and processing adaptability. The volatile profile was significantly reshaped, with marked enrichment of aldehydes and heterocyclic compounds. Through multi-dimensional screening, the pentapeptide FDRGF (TH) was identified with outstanding umami taste and low bitterness. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations confirmed stable binding of TH to immunomodulatory targets, and cellular assays verified that TH improved macrophage metabolic status and regulated the expression of inflammatory mediators under LPS-induced inflammatory conditions. This study elucidates the structure-flavor-activity relationships of sea cucumber protein hydrolysates and identifies a dual-function umami peptide with immunomodulatory activity, providing theoretical support for the value-added utilization of sea cucumber resources.

title: Artificially intelligent modeling of macromolecular assemblies.
authors: Bini, Margherita; Tozzini, Valentina
abstract: The study of macromolecular assembly formation is one of the most challenging tasks in computational modeling as it requires extensive exploration of conformational and configurational space, especially when driven by conformational transitions or folding instabilities, which are typically associated with high energy barriers. Although this type of study has traditionally been addressed in silico by using techniques that reduce the computational cost of simulations, such as coarse-grained models, artificial intelligence (AI) has recently entered the field at multiple levels, aiding in parameter optimization or trajectory analysis and even replacing potentials or force calculations. Recently developed algorithms such as AlphaFold (AF) and RoseTTAFold enable the direct prediction of final structures with high efficiency and confidence, an achievement that earned them the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In this study, we review and analyze the different AI-based strategies used to model protein structure and dynamics and simulate macromolecular assemblies, comparing them with traditional methods, to highlight their respective advantages and limitations. By placing these approaches along an ideal continuum in which accuracy increases as interpretability decreases, we show that hybrid solutions and combinations of methods can be devised to maximize their strengths. Finally, we perspectively outline practical strategies for implementing such integrated approaches in a coherent manner, preserving accuracy and feasibility while maintaining insight into aggregation pathways, intermediate structures, and the molecular mechanisms underlying the phenomenon.

title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis.
authors: Tran, Jenny U; Martinez, Thyandra A; Jurich, Christopher; Josling, Margaret R; Zhang, Julian M; Ayres-Galhardo, Pedro H; Meiler, Jens; Yang, Zhongyue J; MacGurn, Jason A; Brown, Breann L
abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics of Saccharomyces cerevisiae ALAS (scALAS) upon substrate binding. We identified critical conformational changes that occur during catalysis, regulating enzyme activity and protein-protein interactions specific to eukaryotic heme synthesis. Using evolution-guided engineering, we generated scALAS variants with altered catalytic activity and cellular metabolic profiles. Our findings reveal molecular and structural mechanisms underlying heme synthesis regulation and establish a framework for developing targeted therapeutics to treat heme-deficiency disorders and inform a rational design of next-generation therapeutic tools.

title: A "knob-in-hole" gate in the antibody C(H)1 domain underlies subclass-independent IgA hinge cleavage by the commensal metallopeptidase IgAse.
authors: Sebastian Ramirez-Larrota, Juan; Estivill, Guillem Arasa; Lopez-Martin, Mario; Effantin, Gregory; Gragera, Marcos; Sorzano, Carlos Oscar Sanchez; Marcos, Enrique; Eckhard, Ulrich; Gomis-Ruth, Francesc Xavier
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Human immunoglobulin (Ig) A (IgA) protects  approximately 400 m(2) of mucosae from microbes. Bacterial IgA-peptidases subvert this defense by cleaving the F(ab)-F(c) hinge of subclass IgA1 while sparing the hinge-divergent, colon-dominant IgA2 subclass. The exception is IgAse, a  approximately 140-kDa, seven-domain, membrane-bound metallopeptidase from the colonic commensal Thomasclavelia ramosa that targets both subclasses but no other protein. We previously narrowed the minimal functional assembly down to the IgAse catalytic and wrapping domains (CD and WD) plus the IgA1/2 F(ab)', i.e., the hinge and a F(ab) of light and heavy chains (LC, HC), each with a variable and a constant Ig domain (V(L) + C(L), V(H) + C(H)1). The transient interaction culminates in cleavage of a proline-valine bond within the first two hinge residues, downstream of a conserved C-terminal C(H)1 disulfide (SS2). Here, single-particle cryoelectron microscopy of a disulfide-stabilized minimal IgAse:IgA2 F(ab)' complex yielded high-quality density strongly supporting two states along the cleavage reaction coordinate, a "recognition complex" and a subsequent "precatalytic complex," in which F(ab)' binds frontally to the IgAse CD via a C(H)1 beta-sheet and overhang loop LbetaEbetaF. This loop binds like a knob to a preformed hole in the active-site cleft. Binding rearranges the knob and rotates SS2  approximately  180 degrees , enabling access of the hinge into the cleft of the otherwise unaffected precatalytic complex. Together, this work defines a unique, C(H)1-mediated hinge-delivering "gate" mechanism, validated by a crystal structure of unbound IgA2 F(ab), point mutations disrupting the C(H)1:CD interface, and molecular dynamics calculations, which provide the structural framework for subclass-independent IgA cleavage.

title: Computer-aided development of novel thiazolidinone-thiazole derivatives: multidimensional structure-activity relationships revealed by quantum chemical analysis, molecular docking and biological investigation.
authors: Iqbal, Tayyiaba; Khan, Shoaib; Khan, Asrar; Sajjad, Hassnain; Almalki, Masi A; Abid, Souhir; Abid, Majdi; Ali, Syed Kashif; Bakridin, Zaripov; Baltabay, Eshmuratov; Gomha, Sobhi M; Zaki, Magdi E A
abstract: Diabetes mellitus is a major global health challenge, highlighting the need for new inhibitors of the carbohydrate-hydrolyzing enzymes alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase. In this study, a series of thiazole-based thiazolidinone derivatives (1-10) was designed, synthesized, and structurally characterized using spectroscopic techniques. Among the synthesized compounds, 8 showed the strongest inhibitory activity against alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase, with IC(50) values of 5.50 +/- 0.40 and 5.90 +/- 0.10 microM, respectively, and compared with 10.80 +/- 0.50 and 11.10 +/- 0.30 microM for acarbose. Molecular docking suggested that compound 8 can adopt a favorable binding orientation within the active sites of both enzymes through hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic contacts. Enzyme kinetic studies further characterized its mode of inhibition. DFT calculations were performed to examine the electronic properties, frontier molecular orbitals, and molecular electrostatic potential of selected derivatives. ADMET analysis was also conducted to provide preliminary insight into their predicted pharmacokinetic and toxicity-related properties. Overall, the experimental and computational findings identify compound 8 as a promising lead structure for further investigation as an alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase inhibitor.

title: 3D electron diffraction reveals piracetam Form VI two decades after its computational prediction.
authors: Nowak, Maurycy E; Modrzejewski, Marcin; Lanza, Arianna; Svard, Michael; Malinska, Maura; Madsen, Anders O; Krzeszczakowska, Joanna; Syty, Krystyna; Pham, Khanh Ngoc; Hoser, Anna A
abstract: Crystal structure prediction often yields low-energy structures that lack experimental structural confirmation. Using 3D electron diffraction, we resolve predicted piracetam Form VI from a nanocrystalline powder mixture. Free-energy calculations place Form VI among ambient-accessible polymorphs and highlight machine-learning interatomic potentials as scalable tools for finite-temperature polymorph ranking.

title: Protein Language Models Identify Early Folding Residues as Critical Hotspots for Pathogenic Variants and Cancer Prognosis.
authors: Guo, Lisha; Yuan, Fuchong; Zhou, Na; Zhao, Minghui; Liu, Ruotong; Jing, Ming; Feenstra, K Anton; Hou, Qingzhen
abstract: Identifying the specific residues that initiate protein folding is critical for understanding protein stability and the mechanisms of misfolding-related diseases. However, the systematic, proteome-wide identification of these early folding residues (EFRs) has been hampered by both experimental and computational limitations. Here, we present LMEFold, a deep learning framework using protein language models (PLMs) to accurately predict EFRs from amino acid sequence alone. LMEFold outperforms existing sequence-based predictors on the Start2Fold benchmark (ROC AUC = 0.831), and its predicted scores show consistent associations with independent HDX-NMR protection-factor measurements, providing complementary biophysical evidence. Applying LMEFold to annotate over 6.6 million variants across diverse genomic datasets, we find that pathogenic mutations curated in ClinVar are significantly enriched within EFRs (~17%) compared to millions of population variants from large-scale cohorts including the UKB and gnomAD databases (~10%, P < 0.001). Critically, in the MSK-MET pan-cancer clinical cohort, EFR mutations are associated with severe functional disruption and significantly reduced overall patient survival. Structural analysis of hotspot cancer mutations, such as TP53 p.Y163C, suggests a mechanism whereby these variants destabilize protein structure by disrupting the early folding core. Our work establishes EFRs as critical sites of pathogenic vulnerability and provides a powerful framework for the rapid identification of folding-centric prognostic markers using sequence only.

title: Conformational Sampling of CPT1A Enables Dynamic Structure-Based Ligand Screening.
authors: Zhang, Sijia; Zhang, Yingbo; Zhao, Jiasheng; Long, Jiangang; Zhang, Lei; Yang, Zhiwei
abstract: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) catalyzes a rate-limiting step in fatty acid beta-oxidation and is a target for studies of metabolic disease and cancer. However, the structural dynamics of CPT1A remain poorly understood due to the lack of full-length structure. In this study, we employed an integrated computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Markov state models (MSMs), and binding free energy calculations to elucidate the conformational landscape of human CPT1A. We performed an all-atom MD simulation of CPT1A embedded in a realistic outer mitochondrial membrane, and root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF)-guided local region analysis coupled with MSM transition-path analysis and GROMOS clustering convergently identified a representative conformation. The pathway probabilities reported here describe dominant local transitions within specific mobile segments rather than the global equilibrium population of the full-length protein. Using this representative conformation, we performed a virtual screening of over 1.23 million compounds from the ChemDiv library, followed by Lipinski filtering, yielding five candidates with docking scores below -10 kcal/mol. Subsequent MD simulations and binding free energy calculations confirmed stable binding, with Compound 2 exhibiting the most favorable free energy of -25.99 kcal/mol. Principal component analysis (PCA) and secondary-structure analyses revealed ligand-specific modulation of CPT1A dynamics. A preliminary in vitro CPT1 activity assay revealed candidate-specific responses, and the free-energy and activity data were partially consistent. These results provide a dynamically informed structural basis for CPT1A ligand recognition, identify candidates with distinct energetic and functional profiles, and establish an integrated strategy for ligand discovery in structurally uncharacterized proteins.

title: Thermostable Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes for High-Temperature Biomass Conversion: From Molecular Design to Process Integration.
authors: Hu, Yueli; Yang, Xi; Wang, Tianqi; Zheng, Mingshu; Jiang, Zhenghao; Dou, Xinyue; Ren, Xinkun; Wu, Jiaxin
abstract: High-temperature processing of carbohydrate-rich biomass, including starch liquefaction and lignocellulose saccharification, can improve sugar yields, reduce contamination risks, and facilitate integration with thermochemical pretreatments. However, the operational stability of native carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) at 60-90  degrees C remains a major bottleneck for efficient and economically viable biorefineries, and existing reviews rarely integrate multiscale molecular mechanisms with process-relevant engineering strategies. This review systematically examines the multiscale basis of thermostability in CAZymes-covering core hydrophobic packing, electrostatic and metal-mediated networks, disulfide bonds, conformational dynamics, and modular architectures involving catalytic domains, linkers, and carbohydrate-binding modules-and directly links these features to enzyme longevity under high-solids, inhibitor-rich conditions. We then critically compare key engineering strategies, including structure-guided rational design, semi-rational directed evolution, consensus design, ancestral sequence reconstruction, and machine learning-assisted workflows embedded in design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycles, highlighting their respective strengths, limitations, and complementarity. Representative case studies demonstrate that engineered thermophilic alpha-amylases and cellulases achieving DeltaT(m) improvements of approximately 10-20  degrees C can sustain >80-85% residual activity after prolonged exposure at process-relevant temperatures, translating into tangible benefits such as 15-30% reductions in enzyme dosing and measurable decreases in steam consumption, alongside higher sugar titers. By bridging molecular determinants, engineering paradigms, and quantitative process performance, this review provides a pragmatic roadmap for deploying thermostable CAZymes as robust biocatalysts in sustainable high-temperature biomass conversion.

title: Residue-Level Energetic Analysis of Transient Misfolding in the Whirlin PDZ Tandem Reveals a Possible Connection to an AlphaFold-Predicted Alternative Topology.
authors: Pennacchietti, Valeria; Di Felice, Mariana; Toso, Julian; Ventura, Eduarda Santos; Caldarelli, Laura; Toto, Angelo; Malagrino, Francesca; Gianni, Stefano
abstract: Multidomain proteins may populate transient misfolded states that compete with productive folding, but the molecular determinants of these intermediates remain poorly understood. Using the tandem PDZ domains of the scaffolding protein whirlin, in which a misfolded intermediate accumulates only when both domains are denatured, we combined systematic mutagenesis with a thermodynamic framework analogous to double-mutant cycle analysis. Analysis of ~70 mutations identified residues displaying significant non-additive energetic effects, defining an interaction network concentrated within the connecting hairpins, PDZ2, and a few positions at the PDZ1 interface. Interestingly, AlphaFold predicted an alternative domain-swapped topology differing from the experimentally determined structure primarily within these same regions. Although the experimental data do not establish the structure of the misfolded intermediate, this correspondence suggests that the predicted alternative topology may provide a possible structural interpretation of the experimentally identified energetic determinants. Our findings provide a residue-level characterization of the energetic determinants of transient misfolding in a multidomain protein and suggest a possible connection between these determinants and alternative structural arrangements.

title: DFT, Molecular Docking, and Molecular Dynamics Analysis of Electronic Structure, Reactivity, and PTP1B Binding of Phenylacetic and Benzylmalonic Acid-Functionalized C(60) Derivatives.
authors: Rodriguez-Celestino, Veronica; Cisneros-Garcia, Zuriel Natanael; Rodriguez-Zavala, Jaime Gustavo; Mendez-Barrientos, Carlos Ivan; Facio-Munoz, Jose Guadalupe
abstract: Water-soluble C(60) derivatives functionalized with phenylacetic acid (PhAA) and benzylmalonic acid (BnMA), together with their di- and tetrahydroxylated derivatives, were investigated using density functional theory, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate their electronic structure, local and global reactivity, and interactions with protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B). Successive hydroxylation steps were thermodynamically favorable, while electronic structure and reactivity analyses indicated that the fullerene cage retains features compatible with further ROS-related reactivity after hydroxylation. Electrostatic potential analysis revealed differentiated polarity between the fullerene and functionalization regions. Docking showed functionalization-dependent binding modes: PhAA-derived systems sampled both peripheral regions near the WPD and R loops and the catalytic pocket, whereas BnMA-derived systems consistently occupied the catalytic site and interacted with key residues, including Cys215 and Arg221. Molecular dynamics showed reduced flexibility in functionally relevant regions, reorganization of correlated motions, and average catalytic-pocket conformations that were more open than in apo-PTP1B. Overall, these results support the potential of these derivatives for ROS-related reactivity and modulation of PTP1B, although experimental validation is required to establish their biological activity.

title: Structural transition of the immature poxvirus scaffold from preassembly to the scaffold lattice.
authors: Jang, Yeontae; Kim, Seungmi; Lee, Seu-Na; Ryu, Bumhan; Jeong, Hyeongseop; Kang, Eun Sung; Sul, Jae Hoon; Bae, Hayeon; Kim, Yong Ho; Jo, Dong-Gyu; Hyun, Jaekyung
abstract: During poxvirus morphogenesis, the external scaffold defines the shape and size of immature virions. However, its structural characterization has been hindered by the pleomorphic nature of authentic virus particles. Here, we present single-particle cryo-electron microscopy and cryo-electron tomography structures of two distinct in vitro assemblies of the vaccinia virus scaffold protein D13 that recapitulate oligomeric states previously observed in situ. These structures reveal a dramatic transition from rod-like oligomers, representing a pre-assembly state, to a fully formed scaffold, triggered by the docking of the N-terminal peptide of the viral membrane protein A17 into the base cavity of D13. We propose that this interaction destabilizes the pre-assembly conformation and initiates scaffold formation upon viral membrane recruitment, ultimately leading to the formation of immature virions. Our findings provide structural insights into the early stages of poxvirus morphogenesis and establish a mechanistic link between conformational changes in D13 and scaffold assembly.

title: Programming biological behavior with AI-guided de novo protein design.
authors: Huettemann, Philipp; Kortemme, Tanja
abstract: Driven by advances in artificial intelligence, de novo protein design can now generate diverse molecular functions from the ground up, achieving remarkable success in engineering binders against many macromolecular targets. Here, we provide a perspective on how de novo design can progress beyond bimolecular interactions toward the bottom-up construction of protein reaction networks. We highlight how programmable, modular, and controllable de novo components can drive complex, emergent biological behaviors. Overcoming current challenges-including designable protein dynamics, multi-step functionalities, and non-equilibrium systems-is essential for this transition. With continued foundational method improvements, the field is poised to pioneer precise protein perturbations for systems-level insight and to engineer emergent cellular behaviors like signal amplification, decision-making, and error correction de novo to fundamentally advance synthetic biology, biotechnology, and medicine.

title: Structural compatibility is not enough: Current challenges in protein-protein interaction prediction.
authors: Elofsson, Arne
abstract: Since the introduction of AlphaFold2, AI-driven methods have greatly advanced protein structure and complex prediction. However, the performance varies strongly across interaction classes. The performance drops when dynamics are important and when interactions lack a strong co-evolutionary history. We propose to organize these limitations into distinct regions: interactions that are largely tractable by current methods; interactions in which structural compatibility is ambiguous due to competition, paralogy, or stoichiometry; interactions that lack sufficient co-evolutionary signal; and interactions whose biological relevance depends on cellular context, dynamics, or disorder. These limitations define distinct categories of interaction prediction challenges, each requiring different computational and experimental approaches. Future progress will require methods that rely less on multiple sequence alignments, better distinguish interaction strength and specificity, and move beyond static structure prediction toward modeling interaction landscapes in their cellular contexts.

title: Atomic functional site scaffolding in biopolymers with RFdiffusion3.
authors: Butcher, Jasper; Krishna, Rohith; Mitra, Raktim; Woodbury, Seth M; Kim, Donghyo; Brent, Rafael I; Li, Yanjing; Corley, Nathaniel; Favor, Andrew; Chen, Anqi; Kim, Paul T; Funk, Jonathan; Reinoso, Gabriela Bastidas; Wu, Kejia; Muraishi, Aiko; Eisenach, Helen E; Salike, Saman; Mathis, Simon; Thompson, Tuscan Rock; Ruder, Antonia; Sehgal, Enisha; Kubaney, Andrew; Chen, Jie; Politanska, Yuliya; Coventry, Brian; Zhang, Odin; Hardy, Florence J; Qiang, Bo; Didi, Kieran; Kazman, Maxwell; Schaaf, Lars L; DiMaio, Frank; Baker, David
abstract: The catalytic and other sophisticated functions of biomolecules arise from the placement of many atoms in three-dimensional space. Here, we describe a generative artificial intelligence method for biopolymers, RFdiffusion3 (RFD3), which employs free atom diffusion to satisfy complex sets of atomic constraints more rapidly and accurately than previous methods across several challenges from enzyme design to RNA structure design. We demonstrate experimentally the power of the RFD3 pipeline for enzyme design by designing de novo phosphotriesterases with a complex active site architecture incorporating a carbamylated lysine coordinating two metal ions and zinc proteases specific for the transthyretin protein involved in amyloid diseases; in both cases we obtain active catalysts in zero shot 96 construct design campaigns.

title: Distinct functional open states of the polymodal nociceptor TRPV1.
authors: Lee, Bo Hyun; Li, Shisheng; Vu, Simon; Yao, Zhihao; Tian, Yuhua; Yarov-Yarovoy, Vladimir; Zheng, Jie
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: The polymodal nociceptor TRPV1 integrates diverse physical and chemical stimuli, yet whether these inputs drive a common activated state remains unresolved. Here, we show that TRPV1 activators stabilize functionally distinct open states that yield discrete single-channel conductance levels. These functional states appear to arise from distinct open-pore conformations, as evidenced by anomalous mole fraction effect measurements. Structurally, stimulus-specific changes in pore conformation were directly observed using site-directed fluorescence recordings, consistent with Rosetta-guided structural models. Notably, coactivation by two stimuli markedly slows channel opening rather than producing synergistic acceleration, suggesting potential conformational incompatibility across subunits. Together, these findings define TRPV1 gating as a stimulus-partitioned, multistate process and highlight opportunities for selective modulation of TRPV1 in pain management.

title: From prompts to genomes: A constraint-first framework for AI-driven sequence design across life and viruses.
authors: Wicaksono, Adhityo; Parikesit, Arli Aditya
abstract: A constraint-first framework for future 'prompt-to-genome' AI across Bacteria, Archaea, Eukaryota, and viruses is proposed. Genome-scale models can now generate long DNA sequences, and experimentally viable genome-scale designs have begun to appear, but sequence generation alone does not establish biological feasibility. Constraints should not require designs to remain within natural sequence space; rather, they should define testable boundaries for function, inheritance, lifecycle coherence and safe use, including new-to-nature designs. We propose a two-part system. First, a Constraint Compiler translates natural-language prompts into machine-checkable specifications defining scope, context, objectives, assumptions and governance requirements. Second, a modular Validator Stack (C1-C6) evaluates candidate designs for sequence integrity, gene and regulatory plausibility, genome completeness, comparative coherence, systems-level feasibility, and safety and governance. Extreme prompts serve as stress tests to expose hidden assumptions, conflicting objectives, and refusal points, complemented by adversarial testing and risk assessment. A phased roadmap and community benchmarks are proposed to measure specification accuracy, biological feasibility, robustness, and governance performance. The goal is to move prompt-to-genome systems from impressive generation toward reliable, auditable, and accountable biological design.

title: Structure-based computational prioritization of Emodin-8-glucoside as a candidate ligand for the VEGFR1 kinase domain in the context of placenta previa.
authors: Inan, Deniz; Karagecili, Sinan; Ali, Nouman
abstract: Placenta previa is a serious obstetric condition associated with abnormal placental implantation and hemorrhagic complications, for which no targeted pharmacological therapy is established. This study applied an integrated structure-based computational workflow to explore the intracellular VEGFR1 kinase domain as a candidate molecular target. Twenty-one phytochemicals were screened using AutoDock Vina and MOE, with Emodin-8-glucoside consistently prioritized among the highest-ranked compounds. Redocking of the co-crystallized ligand 8ST reproduced its experimental pose with a heavy-atom RMSD of 1.465 A. Comparative 500 ns molecular dynamics simulations showed persistent binding-site association of Emodin-8-glucoside and the 8ST control. End-point energy estimates were method dependent, with MM-GBSA yielding a negative mean estimate while MM-PBSA yielded a near-zero estimate with substantial variability. DFT analysis produced a HOMO-LUMO gap of 0.13204 Hartree (approximately 3.59 eV). SwissADME and ProTox 3.0 identified low gastrointestinal absorption, P-glycoprotein substrate behavior, high polarity, and several predicted toxicity liabilities. Overall, Emodin-8-glucoside represents an in-silico-prioritized exploratory candidate requiring biochemical, selectivity, placental-cell, and pregnancy-safety validation.

title: Relating gammaD-crystallin conformations to local aggregate topology.
authors: Diessner, Elizabeth M; Freites, J Alfredo; Tobias, Douglas J; Butts, Carter T
abstract: The structural crystallins of the eye lens must persist at high concentrations (up to 600 mg/ml in some species), while remaining solvated within a hydrogel that must endure for the life of the organism. Transient networks of interactions among these proteins may create contacts that facilitate the development of irreversible aggregation, while also contributing to the physical properties of the lens hydrogel. Although arising from complex multibody interactions, these interaction networks also depend upon the conformational states of individual protein monomers; in particular, some states may not be conducive to interaction, while others facilitate the coordination of multiple bound interactions. Here, we use multi-scale simulation to examine networks of interaction for the human lens protein gammaD-crystallin, relating monomeric conformational states to position within the aggregation graph. We identify a three-role system of conformational states, with the formation of large aggregates associated with a highly "promiscuous" set of states whose members readily interact with themselves and others. We discuss the relationship between conformational states and aggregation, considering the two-way influence between intermolecular interactions and the monomeric conformational states. Differences in role occupancies are seen between wild-type gammaD-crystallin and the cataract-associated W42R variant, consistent with the hypothesis that W42R monomers more readily occupy distributions of conformational states that are conducive to the formation of larger aggregates.

title: The MODNAP benchmark set for modeling ribose-based modified nucleic acid and nucleic acid-protein complexes: a case study with AlphaFold 3.
authors: Fu, Jiemin; Milam, Valeria Tohver; McShan, Andrew C
abstract: Modified nucleic acids play important roles in biology and biotechnology. However, their chemical and structural diversity as well as effects on nucleic acid structure and intermolecular interactions remain incompletely characterized. The performance of structure prediction and co-folding algorithms for modeling modified nucleic acids and nucleic acid-protein complexes has also not been evaluated. Here, we systematically analyze ribose-based modified nucleotides present in structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank. Modified nucleotides are primarily localized to the nucleobase, where they exhibit chemical and structural diversity shaped by molecular size, topological shape descriptors, and polarity-related properties. We develop MODNAP, the first curated dataset of experimentally determined structures containing modified nucleotides. Using MODNAP, we benchmark AlphaFold 3 on 1039 nucleic acid and nucleic acid-protein complex structures spanning a range of nucleotide modifications, tertiary folds, and biological functions. AlphaFold 3 achieves success rates exceeding 80% at an RMSD threshold of 2.5 A. However, its accuracy in positioning modified nucleotides is variable and decreases for structures not explicitly represented in training. PoseBusters analysis reveals frequent intramolecular validity failures, primarily due to non-ideal ribose ring geometries. Together, these results establish MODNAP as a resource for evaluating and improving structure prediction methods for modified nucleic acids.

title: Engineering catalytic promiscuity in serum albumin: synergistic roles of microenvironment, structural dynamics, and nano conjugation.
authors: Patra, Swapan; Dey, Nilanjan
abstract: This study investigates the catalytic hydrolysis of p-nitrophenyl acetate (PNPA) in the presence of bovine serum albumin (BSA) as a biocatalyst, with an emphasis on the role of protein conformation, substrate concentration, and environmental factors. Further experiments with varying BSA and PNPA concentrations demonstrated Michaelis-Menten-type kinetics and a positive correlation between BSA concentration and the rate of hydrolysis. This effect was attributed to increased availability of catalytically active histidine residues and potential conformational changes that expose active sites. Comparisons with alpha-lactalbumin and free histidine under similar conditions indicated the superior catalytic efficiency of BSA, due to both crowding effects and its structural microenvironment. The effects of pH, ionic strength, and substrate alkyl chain length were also examined, revealing optimal catalytic activity at pH 7.4 and a significant rate enhancement for substrates with extended hydrophobic regions, likely due to stronger BSA-substrate interactions. Additionally, BSA structural alterations through denaturation, PEGylation, and gold nanoparticle (Au-NPs) conjugation were evaluated, showing varied catalytic performance due to differences in rigidity and nature of microenvironment etc. The molecular docking studies indicated the involvement of not only histidine but also serine and arginine residues in the catalytic activity.

title: Characterization of epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG)-phosphorylated hemoglobin for changing pork meat quality: from simulations to applications.
authors: Wang, Yanli; Liu, Lili; Cheng, Weiwei; Zhang, Xinshuai; Ding, Yue
journal: Journal of the science of food and agriculture
abstract: BACKGROUND: The valorization of hemoglobin (Hb) from meat processing by-products is essential for sustainable recycling. However, this process is severely constrained by the inherent limitations of Hb, such as poor stability and low solubility. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a computationally guided dual-modification strategy. This approach integrates covalent phosphorylation with epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG)-mediated non-covalent interactions to enhance the applicability of modified Hb. RESULTS: Artificial neural network prediction and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to rationalize the modification process. MD simulations and binding energy calculations revealed that the stability of the complex is driven by specific amino acid residues, with ALA142, ASN139 and THR38 making the most significant contributions through robust hydrogen bonding networks. Spectroscopic analysis confirmed that this interaction with EGCG drastically reduced the alpha-helix content (from 74% to 30%), inducing a conformational opening that exposed cryptic hydrophobic pockets. The modified Hb exhibited superior surface hydrophobicity, antioxidant activity and foaming capacity. Crucially, application in a pork meat sausage model demonstrated that the EGCG-phosphorylated porcine hemoglobin (EGCG-PHb) complex effectively acted, overcoming the severe gel brittleness caused by phosphorylation and significantly enhancing the springiness and chewiness of the meat matrix. CONCLUSION: The protein structure of the EGCG-PHb complex was significantly altered compared to Hb, and EGCG-PHb complex also significantly improved the springiness and chewiness of pork sausages. This dual-modification strategy provides new insights into the development and utilization of Hb. (c) 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

title: HDOCK-Multimer: improved structure prediction of large protein complexes by integrating docking and combinatorial assembly.
authors: Yao, Xuan; Ya, Yifan; Li, Hao; Huang, Sheng-You
abstract: Accurate prediction of large protein assembly structures is crucial for understanding biological processes, yet remains a challenge for end-to-end approaches such as AlphaFold owing to their large size and intricate multi-chain interactions. Docking methods can handle large proteins, but suffer from the huge combinatorial binding space of multiple chains. Assembly methods offer an alternative way, but critically rely on the quality of predicted subcomponents. Here we present HDOCK-Multimer (HDM), a framework that integrates docking and combinatorial assembly for structure prediction of large protein complexes. HDM efficiently reduces reliance on subcomponent quality through docking, while leveraging the pairwise interactions of subcomponents through assembly. When evaluated on 3 benchmarks of 35 large heteromeric complexes, 172 large protein complexes and 7 CASP15 targets, HDM substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods including CombFold, MoLPC, AlphaFold-Multimer and AlphaFold3. In addition, HDM also demonstrates the capacity to predict the stoichiometry and model the complex without stoichiometry input.

title: Small viruses reveal bidirectional evolution between HK97-fold viruses and encapsulins via procapsids.
authors: Aguilar, Abelardo; Miranda Perez, Ingrid; Nadel, Omer; Nayfach, Stephen; Ruiz Pestana, Luis; Segall, Anca M; Rohwer, Forest L; Roux, Simon; White, Simon; Luque, Antoni
abstract: The HK97-fold is an ancient, conserved protein structure that assembles protein shells, forming the capsids of Duplodnaviria viruses and prokaryotic biochemical compartments called encapsulsins. It has been proposed that encapsulins evolved from HK97-fold viruses. But the higher complexity of viral capsids represents a biophysical paradox in the evolution of HK97-fold protein shells. To resolve this problem, we hypothesize the existence of simpler HK97-fold viral capsids associated with smaller genomes than those of known HK97-fold viruses. Such small viral genomes are searched in environmental metagenomes across public databases, including IMG/M and MGnify. Using hidden Markov models and protein language models, we identify and characterize small viral genomes encoding HK97-fold proteins that exhibit molecular similarities to encapsulins yet lack portal and tail genes. The phylogenetic analyses of HK97-fold proteins reveal independent mixed groups of viruses and encapsulins, and structural analyses identify similarities between encapsulins and procapsids, the immature state of viral capsids. The observations support a bidirectional evolution between encapsulins and HK97-fold viruses enabled by the viral procapsid state. Using biophysical and genomic arguments, we introduce an evolutionary model of HK97-fold protein shells, predicting that they emerged as lower-symmetry biochemical compartments and that HK97-fold viral capsids may retain biochemical functions.

title: Predicting phase transitions across temperature, pressure, and chemical potential using exponentially tilted thermodynamic maps.
authors: Lee, Suemin; Wang, Ruiyu; Herron, Lukas; Tiwary, Pratyush
abstract: Predicting and characterizing phase transitions is crucial for understanding generic physical phenomena such as crystallization, protein folding, and others. However, directly observing phase transitions is not always easy, and we often have limited observations far from the phase boundary, measured under specific thermodynamic conditions. In this study, we propose a statistical-physics- and generative-AI-driven framework that uses such limited information to generate samples of different phases under arbitrary thermodynamic conditions, which we call Exponentially Tilted Thermodynamic Maps (expTM). The central idea is to map collected data into a simple, tractable prior expressed as an exponentially tilted Gaussian. We demonstrate how the variance and mean of the prior can be correlated with pairs of thermodynamic control variables, including temperature, pressure, and chemical potential. This gives us the ability to generate thermodynamically correct samples under any values of the control variables. To demonstrate the practical applicability of this approach, we use expTM to sample a lattice gas model with the grand canonical ensemble, capturing phase transitions under varying chemical potentials and temperatures. We further demonstrate how expTM can model the isothermal-isobaric ensemble, with which we predict different phases of CO(2) under varying pressure conditions. Both examples are trained on very limited data far from the phase boundary. These results establish expTM as a robust tool for understanding phase transitions across diverse thermodynamic conditions requiring only a small number of observations.

title: Beyond SELEX: AI-driven aptamers from sequence to structure to function.
authors: Cui, Boming; Lian, Xintao; Song, Weiwei; Yang, Hua; Yang, Xiaojuan; Wang, Lan; Yang, Ge
abstract: Conventional aptamer discovery by systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) is often constrained by limited library capacity, PCR bias, and multi-round screening. The recent convergence of artificial intelligence with aptamer development is driving a paradigm shift from empirical screening toward rational, data-driven design. This Review presents a timely and comprehensive overview of AI integration across the entire aptamer development pipeline, with a particular emphasis on advances reported in 2024-2026. We begin by discussing bioinformatics databases and computational tools for high-throughput SELEX data analysis. We then review state-of-the-art strategies for secondary and tertiary structure prediction, including recent breakthroughs such as AlphaFold 3, RoseTTAFoldNA, and diffusion-based approaches. We also cover machine learning methods for aptamer-target interaction prediction, molecular docking, dynamics simulations, and free energy calculations. A major focus is placed on very recent AI-driven generative design, including diffusion models (AptaDiff), language model-based frameworks (InstructNA, GRAPE-LM), and reinforcement learning approaches (AiDTA) for de novo aptamer generation and optimization. Emerging applications of AI-designed aptamers in precision diagnostics, targeted therapy, and biosensing are also surveyed. Finally, we discuss current challenges and outline future directions toward closed-loop, interpretable AI frameworks for translational aptamer development. By synthesizing the latest computational and experimental advances, this Review aims to serve as a timely resource for researchers seeking to leverage AI for next-generation aptamer discovery.

title: RNADaemon: Reinforcement Learning-Guided Molecular Dynamics for RNA Tertiary Structure Prediction.
authors: Xu, Wentao; Wu, You; Yu, Xiang
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: Accurate prediction of RNA tertiary structure remains a central challenge in structural biology, yet existing computational approaches face fundamental limitations arising from the ruggedness of the RNA free-energy landscape and the scarcity of experimentally resolved structures. Here we present RNADaemon, a framework that formulates RNA tertiary structure prediction as a Markov Decision Process and trains a Soft Actor-Critic agent to apply adaptive external force-field biases that steer all-atom molecular dynamics toward native-like conformations to minimize the eRMSD metric. Trained on 479 monomeric RNA structures and evaluated on 14 test cases from CASP16, RNA-Puzzles, and the PDB, the agent trains stably, approaches SimRNA and FARFAR2 in median RMSD, and recovers the global fold of most reference structures. However, performance remains markedly inferior to that of AlphaFold 3 and trRosettaRNA. We identify the scalar Bellman error as a fundamental information bottleneck that currently limits the performance of the agent. To our knowledge, this is the first application of continuous-action deep reinforcement learning (RL) with all-atom force fields to RNA tertiary structure prediction. This study establishes a benchmark for future comparisons and provides diagnostic insights for RL-guided RNA structure modeling.

title: A pseudo-labeling approach for automated assignment of unlabeled proteins exceeding 100 amino acid residues.
authors: Niu, Xiaogang; Hou, Xianhui; Jin, Changwen
abstract: In the era of AI-driven protein structure prediction, there is an urgent demand for rapid, accessible experimental approaches to validate computationally predicted structural models or to improve the accuracy of AI-based structure determination. As a key experimental technique for determining protein structures in solution, conventional biomolecular NMR spectroscopy relies heavily on proteins labeled with (13)C and (15)N isotopes, a requirement that entails high experimental costs, lengthy sample preparation times, and steep technical barriers, thereby limiting its broader application. Building on our previous work, we have developed a pseudo-labeling strategy for the automated resonance assignment of unlabeled proteins. Using high-field NMR spectrometers equipped with cryoprobes, we acquired natural-abundance (1)H-(13)C and (1)H-(15)N heteronuclear correlation spectra directly from unlabeled samples. By integrating predicted chemical shifts of H(N), H(alpha), (13)C(alpha), and (15)N from three complementary AI tools into an iterative simulated annealing framework with an alternating scoring scheme, our method effectively resolves severe cross-peak overlap during the automated assignment process by introducing heteronuclear dimensional constraints. This approach enables reliable automated backbone resonance assignment for unlabeled proteins exceeding 100 amino acid residues. We anticipate that this labeling-free strategy will lower the technical barrier to biomolecular NMR, enabling researchers without specialized NMR expertise to employ NMR spectroscopy in fundamental life science research and drug development.

title: Lab to codes: multimodel advanced AI-driven pipelines to drive antimicrobial peptide design for the post-antibiotic era.
authors: Saleem, Naveed; El-Omar, Emad; Kumar, Naresh; Willcox, Mark; Jiang, Xiao-Tao
journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
abstract: The rapid emergence of global antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has outpaced the development of new antimicrobial agents, necessitating transformative approaches such as AI-driven in-silico drug discovery. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising alternatives due to their broad-spectrum bactericidal activity and limited susceptibility to resistance. However, the transition from bench to bedside remains constrained by certain challenges, such as instability, potency, and cytotoxicity. Here, well-integrated, multi-model AI-driven pipeline strategies for the mining and discovery of novel AMPs are designed to address these concerns through simultaneous multi-purpose optimization. The proposed architectural frameworks combine discriminative AMP classifiers, quantitative potency, and cytotoxicity screening filters to prioritize AMPs with good efficacy and safety profiles. To ensure novelty, the pipeline integrates multi-layer sequential and genomic screening by adopting alignment and profile-based approaches. Structural refinements are achieved through advanced molecular docking (MD) and protein folding approaches, providing mechanistic insights regarding peptide-target interactions. In parallel, enzymatic susceptibility and stability prediction models are incorporated to optimize AMP pharmacokinetic potentials. Notably, the multi-objective pipeline operates within iterative optimization loops; discriminative and generative AI models and sequential redesign strategies refine candidates based on multi-purpose closed feedback loops across stability, novelty, efficacy, and toxicity outcomes. These systematic and integrated approaches overcome key bottlenecks associated with traditional linear drug discovery, potentially reducing late-stage attrition and accelerating the transformation from in-silico predictions to wet-lab validation. Collectively, this review provides reproducible and generalizable blueprints for next-generation antimicrobial agents, demonstrating the computational potentials of AI-driven, multi-model architectural frameworks to tackle the global AMR crisis and favour precision design of AMPs with better therapeutic indices.

title: Programmable synthetic engineering of adaptive microbial cell factories: from amide transforming enzymes to advanced biocatalytic systems.
authors: Fatima, Syeda Warisul; Alam, Shahenvaz
abstract: Microbial cell factories integrate metabolic engineering, synthetic regulation, protein engineering, and computational design to improve catalytic performance and process robustness. Within this landscape, amide transforming enzymes provide diverse functions ranging from nitrogen metabolism and hydrolysis to covalent protein remodeling. This review examines amidases, asparaginases, glutaminases, nitrilases, nitrile hydratases, acylases, and carbamylases, with particular emphasis on microbial transglutaminase (MTGase). MTGase is distinguished by its ability to catalyze covalent epsilon-(gamma-glutamyl) lysine crosslinking through acyl transfer reactions, enabling protein stabilization, molecular assembly, immobilization, and spatial organization of catalytic systems. This review critically examines the transition from classical amide transforming enzymes toward engineered biocatalytic systems and evaluates how MTGase could be leveraged as a protein level control component in microbial cell factories. Experimental developments in MTGase production, structural and protein engineering, synthetic genetic circuits, CRISPR based regulation, metabolic control, nanobiomaterials, and spatial biocatalysis are evaluated alongside computational approaches including AlphaFold assisted structure prediction, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, machine learning guided mutagenesis, and metabolic modeling. Emphasis is placed on experimentally validated outcomes and current limitations. Key unresolved barriers include intracellular off target crosslinking, proteostatic burden, variable crosslink stoichiometry, limited temporal control of MTGase activity, chassis dependence, and industrial scale up. Where direct evidence is lacking, prospective applications are distinguished from established capabilities and corresponding engineering strategies are proposed. Collectively, this review envisions MTGase as a controllable protein level platform for synthetic biology, while defining the evidence, limitations, and experimental requirements needed for its broader application in microbial biotechnology.

title: Single-Molecule Force Spectroscopy: Experiments, Analysis, and Simulations.
authors: Mesbah, Ismahene; Sumbul, Fidan; Valotteau, Claire; Rico, Felix
abstract: The mechanical properties of cells and subcellular components are important for a mechanistic understanding of biological processes. The quantification of the mechanics of cells and biomolecules using biophysical methods has matured thanks to the development of nanotechnologies such as optical and magnetic tweezers, the biomembrane force probe and atomic force microscopy (AFM). Force spectroscopy allows the determination of the forces required to unfold protein domains and to disrupt individual receptor/ligand bonds. Analytical models allow a phenomenological characterization of the underlying energy landscape. Molecular dynamics simulations allow the study of similar biological processes in atomic detail. In this chapter, we first provide a roadmap of force spectroscopy measurement and analysis and its interpretation in terms of available theories. We then present the background for molecular dynamics simulations, focusing on steered molecular dynamics (SMD) and the importance of bridging computational tools and theoretical frameworks with experimental techniques. We finally provide a step-by-step protocol of AFM-based and SMD experiments.

title: Leveraging high-throughput proteomics and AI-based protein folding to accelerate VAV1 molecular glue discovery.
authors: Lin, Hanfeng; Yu, Xin; Zheng, Haiyang; Cheng, Ran; Zhang, Min; Qi, Xiaoli; Yang, Yen-Yu; Zhou, Shengmin; Qi, Rui; Le, Ly; Bortolato, Andrea; Yesylevskyy, Semen; Nafiiev, Alan; Che, Xing; Wang, Jin
abstract: This study reports a series of CRBN molecular glues that selectively induce proteasomal degradation of VAV1, a hematopoietic-specific signaling protein and key target in hematological malignancies and autoimmune diseases. Using unbiased global proteomics, we identify phenyl-glutarimide derivatives (e.g., NGT-201-12) as effective VAV1 degraders that engage its C-terminal SH3 domain (SH3-2). We elucidate a non-canonical RT-loop degron (RDxS motif, residues 796-799) in SH3-2, distinct from previously characterized G-loop degrons, supported by the physics- and AI-driven GluePlex workflow and site-directed mutagenesis. Applying Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) to predicted ternary structures yields cooperativity metrics that correlate with degradation potency, overcoming limitations of standard docking and enabling prospective ranking of analogs-even from weak initial binders. We further show that conformational restriction via halogen substitution (e.g., NGT-201-18) potentiates degradation, a principle rationalized by DFT calculations, while comprehensive SAR studies chart a roadmap for next-generation degraders. Dose-response proteomics confirms VAV1 as the primary target and reveals LIMD1, bearing a canonical G-loop, as an off-target, showing that one glue can engage disparate degrons. These findings expand the landscape of CRBN neosubstrate recognition and offer a therapeutic strategy for targeting VAV1.

title: Functional alignment of protein language models via reinforcement learning.
authors: Blalock, Nathaniel; Seshadri, Srinath; Nakamura, Kensuke; Babbar, Agrim; Fahlberg, Sarah A; Kulkarni, Ameya; Romero, Philip A
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) enable generative design of novel protein sequences but remain fundamentally misaligned with protein engineering goals, as they lack explicit understanding of function and often fail to improve properties beyond those found in nature. We introduce Reinforcement Learning from eXperimental Feedback (RLXF), a general framework that aligns protein language models with experimentally measured functional objectives, drawing inspiration from the methods used to align large language models like ChatGPT. Applied across five diverse protein families, RLXF improves generation of high-functioning variants beyond pre-trained baselines. We demonstrate this with CreiLOV, an oxygen-independent fluorescent protein, where RLXF-aligned models generate sequences with significantly enhanced fluorescence, including the most fluorescent CreiLOV variants reported to date. Our results indicate that RLXF-aligned models effectively integrate the evolutionary knowledge encoded in pre-trained pLMs with experimental observations, improving the success rate of generated sequences and enabling the discovery of synergistic mutation combinations that are difficult to identify through zero-shot or evolutionary approaches. RLXF provides a scalable and accessible approach to steer generative models toward desired biochemical properties, enabling function-driven protein design beyond the limits of natural evolution.

title: Reprogramming the Rossmann fold signature motif creates orthogonal redox biocatalysts.
authors: Ping, Yu; Kim, Jin Young; Dinh, Minh-Anh L; Luu, Emma; Worakaensai, Suphanida; Zhang, Shiding; Black, William B; Monge, Emma; Ng, Hans Jefferson C; Perea, Sean; Zhang, Yulai; Cui, Youtian; King, Edward; Siegel, Justin B; Li, Han
abstract: Biological reducing power is carried by nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (phosphate) (NAD(P)/H), which supports cellular functions and cannot be specifically directed to engineered metabolic pathways. Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN(H)) has emerged as an orthogonal redox cofactor to address this. Herein, to create NMN(H)-specific enzymes that no longer interact with cellular NAD(P)/H pools, we perturb the ancient, conserved GxGxxG motif in Rossmann fold enzymes that enables persistent NAD(P)/H recognition. We build variants NRC-01 and NRC-02 on phosphite dehydrogenase (PTDH), which eliminate electron leaking to NAD(P)H-dependent side reactions while driving NMNH-dependent biotransformation with ~240-fold higher productivity than existing catalysts. Testing the design principle on 12 other vastly diverse enzymes yields additional NMN(H)-orthogonal enzymes catalyzing valuable biomanufacturing reactions, and reveals a potential rule predicting the translatability of this method. Rosetta modeling, structural alignment, and experimental results reveal that Rossmann fold reprogramming, paired with engineered structural reinforcement, may offer a general route to orthogonal redox biocatalysts.

title: Structural basis of the gating mechanism of the large-conductance mechanosensitive channel from Escherichia coli.
authors: Hardman, Katie; Wort, Joshua L; Waheed, Qaiser; Liu, Xinyu; Arul, Diya; Porav, Sebastian A; Calabrese, Antonio N; Muench, Stephen P; Pliotas, Christos
abstract: The mechanosensitive channel of large conductance (MscL) is a tension-gated, pore-forming protein that acts as a safety valve to protect bacteria from osmotic lysis. Escherichia coli MscL (EcMscL) was the first mechanosensitive channel discovered and subsequently served as a model system for understanding mechanical sensing, becoming one of the most decorated and well-studied systems. Despite extensive biophysical and functional characterisation spanning several decades, the precise mechanism of EcMscL gating has been poorly understood due to the lack of high-resolution structural information. Herein, we solve two EcMscL structures by cryoEM in the closed conformation in DMPC and DOPC lipid nanodiscs. Using PELDOR/DEER spectroscopy, we screen conditions and identify that in DSPC lipids, the EcMscL conformational ensemble shifts away from the closed state and that open-like states are present. We solve the structure in an expanded state by cryoEM, revealing an architecture with pore properties consistent with previous electrophysiology reports. By combining hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry and molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the dynamics of EcMscL gating in lipid bilayers, identifying sites involved in the closed-to-expanded transition. Combined, this enables us to inform on the elusive structural mechanism of EcMscL mechanosensitive channel function.

title: Complexation of soybean beta-conglycinin and glycinin with phytic acid: Molecular insights and effects on structural and digestive properties.
authors: Zhang, Yujiao; Fei, Chengxin; Zhao, Ruojie; Dai, Oujun; Deng, Zhixiong; Fan, Bei; Wang, Fengzhong; Huang, Yatao
abstract: This study investigated the complexation of phytic acid (PA) with soybean beta-conglycinin (7S) and glycinin (11S) and its effects on protein structure and digestibility. Complex formation was most pronounced near pH 3.0, accompanied by decreased solubility and enhanced aggregation. PA binding reduced beta-sheet content from 36.0% to 31.4% in 7S and from 37.3% to 35.1% in 11S, indicating conformational rearrangement. During simulated gastric digestion, hydrolysis decreased from 10.59% to 7.42% for 7S and from 9.93% to 6.92% for 11S, whereas hydrolysis increased during subsequent intestinal digestion. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations provided theoretical support for interpreting the experimental observations, suggesting contributions from electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonding, with more extensive contacts predicted for PA-11S. Isothermal titration calorimetry confirmed a higher affinity of PA for 11S, with dissociation constants of 12.3 muM for 11S and 32.5 muM for 7S. At pH 3.0 and 37  degrees C, binding was enthalpically and entropically favorable for 7S but enthalpy-driven for 11S. These findings provide molecular insights into PA-soy protein interactions and their implications for protein hydrolysis during simulated gastrointestinal digestion.

title: Missense3D: leveraging protein structures, including AlphaFold models, to understand the effect of missense variants.
authors: Tsitsa, Ifigenia; Hanna, Gordon; Conev, Anja; Islam, Suhail A; Sternberg, Michael Je; David, Alessia
abstract: The growing availability of 3D protein structures enables large-scale assessment of missense variants and their phenotypic impact. Missense3D, first developed in 2019, predicts the structural consequences of amino acid substitutions and provides mechanistic explanations by identifying features such as cavities, steric clashes and disrupted non-covalent bonds that may cause protein misfolding. The new Missense3D algorithm presented here accepts genomics, protein, and structural coordinates; models variants on both single proteins and protein-protein complexes using experimental and predicted structures, including AlphaFold models; performs automated sequence-structure mapping; and evaluates structural model quality before analysis. The Missense3D web server is freely available to all users, including commercial ones, at https://missense3d.bc.ic.ac.uk/~missense3d2/.

title: Protein interactions with small molecules, peptides and proteins share residue cluster classes.
authors: Hernandez Castillo, Juan Martin; Vilchis Macias, Erik Hazel; Del Rio, Gabriel
abstract: Macromolecular interactions with small molecules, peptides, and proteins are fundamental to cellular function. Despite intensive efforts to identify small-molecule modulators of protein-protein interactions (PPIs), successfully targeted interfaces remain rare, reinforcing the premise that binding sites across these molecular scale regimes possess distinct structural architectures. We previously demonstrated that the densest topological regions of protein structures, categorized as a collection of Residue Cluster Classes (cRCC), can effectively classify global protein folds and PPI. Here, we leverage the cRCC framework to train machine learning models to classify peptide-protein interactions. The top-performing algorithms achieved near 100% classification accuracy, with minimal overfitting (<2%). To ensure model generalizability, these optimized algorithms were cross-tested on independent datasets to identify both protein-protein and protein-small-molecule interfaces, maintaining a 95% average success rate and validating the robust predictive reliability of our approach. Collectively, these findings show that cRCC constitute intensive structural properties of protein interfaces, remaining invariant to the molecular weight of the interacting partner. Consequently, this framework provides a novel computational strategy to prioritize druggable PPI targets for small-molecule discovery and guide the rational design of synthetic protein interfaces.

title: Evolution, structural diversity and functional plasticity of plant derived multifunctional proteases and alpha-amylases inhibitors.
authors: Dongare, Pratiksha M; Madage, Varsha A; Deshpande, Neha V; Giri, Ashok P; Pawar, Pankaj K
abstract: Plant derived multifunctional inhibitors (MFIs) are an important class of plant defense proteins that disrupt insect digestion by simultaneously impairing protein and carbohydrate catabolism. With the increasing knowledge of inhibitors of plant enzymes, MFIs have become a separate functional group. In this review we propose an extended definition that encompasses the classical inhibitors acting on structurally unrelated enzymes and also inhibitors acting on enzymes of the same substrate pathway, e.g. alpha-amylase/alpha-glucosidase and trypsin/chymotrypsin systems. Most of the MFIs consist of single polypeptide chains with spatially separated inhibitory sites, which allow simultaneous inhibition of several enzyme targets. The structural organization, inhibitory mechanism and evolutionary diversification of these inhibitors are reviewed with emphasis on the major families including Bowman-Birk, Kunitz-type and cereal trypsin/alpha-amylase inhibitors. Their domain architecture, disulfide bond patterns and structure-function relationships are discussed in view of their remarkable stability and functional versatility. Recent advances in computational structural biology, including molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and AlphaFold-based protein structure prediction, have promoted mechanistic insights and enabled structure-guided engineering of improved inhibitors. The review also discusses the evolutionary origin of MFIs through gene duplication, domain shuffling, sequence diversification and adaptive evolution, and emerging approaches such as protein engineering, recombinant expression, synthetic biology and genome editing. Finally, the applications in crop protection, development of biopesticides and food biotechnology, as well as the challenges regarding insect adaptation, evolution of resistance, biosafety and ecological impacts are critically discussed. Bridging current gaps in structural characterization and in vivo validation is necessary for the translation of MFIs into sustainable agricultural and biotechnological applications.

title: Correction: Simulation of protein structure using a coarse-grained potential incorporating the backbone dihedral interactions.
authors: Kole, Kanika; Ghosh Moulick, Abhik; Chakrabarti, Jaydeb
abstract: Correction for 'Simulation of protein structure using a coarse-grained potential incorporating the backbone dihedral interactions' by Kanika Kole et al., Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys., 2026, 28, 23541-23554, https://doi.org/10.1039/d6cp02188c.

title: Benchmarking AI-driven protocols for cyclic peptide conformer prediction and ranking.
authors: Damjanovic, Jovan; Ochoa, Rodrigo
abstract: Generative AI is being used in peptide design to optimize binders from early research stages. One notable application is with respect to cyclic peptides, wherein AI assists in modelling conformers in bound or solution states. This work benchmarks state-of-the-art protocols' ability to predict and rank conformers of cyclic peptide binders alone and in complex with their targets, using sequence or all-atom representations. The datasets consist of cyclic peptides with experimental structures available in public repositories. Various tools were included in the benchmark: HighFold, cyclic-aware AlphaFold2 as implemented in EvoBind2, CycPepDock, Boltz-1/1x, Boltz-2, and Chai-1. We found that more recent tools provide a structure prediction advantage over their AlphaFold2-based counterparts, although accurate results with both sets of tools are largely limited to protein-peptide complexes, rather than the free solution structure. In addition, using a cyclic relative positional encoding offset proved key for accurate prediction, and the natural amino acid representation was found to outperform the more general SMILES string input. We mirror prior literature findings on linear peptides by showing that even for accurate predictions, model confidence metrics poorly correlate with experimentally observed binding affinity. Lastly, we compare the performance of AI-based tools to that of physics-based simulations, showing that the latter remain the only way to account for intrinsic conformational flexibility of cyclic peptides, but that the former have a significant price/performance advantage in complex structure prediction. This study provides insights applicable to the design and optimization of cyclic peptides, contributing to advancements in peptide-based therapeutics.

title: Rare missense variants identified by whole-genome sequencing in men with oligoasthenoteratozoospermia: An experimental study.
authors: Sadeghzadeh, Sara; Malcher, Agnieszka; Ebrahimi Askari, Razieh; Sefid, Fatemeh; Ibrahim, Rim; Pastuszak, Krzysztof; Srivastava, Aashish; Dehghani, Mohammadreza; Vahidi, Serajoddin; Lotfi, Marzieh; Ghasemi, Nasrin; Kurpisz, Maciej
abstract: BACKGROUND: Oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OAT) is a major cause of male infertility, characterized by low sperm count, poor motility, and abnormal morphology. While genetic factors contribute to a substantial proportion of cases, the specific variants underlying OAT remain largely unknown, especially in populations with high rates of consanguinity. OBJECTIVE: To identify rare candidate variants potentially associated with OAT using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) in 7 men from consanguineous families. MATERIALS AND METHODS: 7 men with OAT from consanguineous families, with normal karyotypes and no Y-chromosome microdeletions, were selected. WGS was performed, and variants were called using DeepVariant. These variants were then annotated using the Ensembl variant effect predictor. Rare variants were prioritized based on their predicted pathogenicity and relevance to reproduction, and candidate variants were validated. Protein structure modeling and analysis of mutation-induced effects on molecular interactions were carried out using Swiss model and AlphaFold. RESULTS: We identified 2 rare homozygous missense variants in DNAH9 (p.Pro355Leu) and CFAP45 (p.Arg493Trp) in the index case with OAT. Both genes have been implicated in sperm flagellar structure and motility. Additional variants in genes associated with spermiogenesis, acrosomal integrity, and testicular function were also identified. CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrate the potential utility of WGS in identifying rare candidate variants potentially associated with OAT. The identified DNAH9 and CFAP45 variants, together with additional candidate variants, may contribute to the impaired sperm function observed in this man. This study also highlights the value of genome-wide analyses in improving our understanding of male infertility, particularly in consanguineous populations, and provides a foundation for future functional studies and personalized diagnostic approaches.

title: Discovery of a Potent and Selective First-In-Class Antagonist of GPR15 With In Vivo Anti-Obesity Activity.
authors: Huang, Chong; Qiao, Jingxin; Zhou, Mengqiu; Yang, Xin; Zhu, Lengjing; Ru, Jinxiao; Du, Le; Liu, Wuxin; Chen, Yan; Xia, Anjie; Li, Linli; Yang, Shengyong
abstract: GPR15 (G Protein-coupled Receptor 15), an atypical chemokine receptor, is implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple diseases, yet small-molecule GPR15 antagonists remain undeveloped. Herein, we identify and characterize YL410, the first-in-class potent and selective GPR15 antagonist. In the cAMP-GloSensor assay, YL410 inhibits GPR15 with an IC(50) of 0.027 +/- 0.005 microM, and displays high selectivity against a panel of related GPCRs and kinases. It suppresses GPR15L-induced Jurkat T-cell migration, and exhibits favorable pharmacokinetics and acceptable safety. Molecular docking, replicated molecular dynamics simulations, quantitative contact analyses, and mutagenesis experiments support a plausible orthosteric binding model for YL410, maintained by a reproducible network of polar and hydrophobic contacts, which rationalizes its potent antagonism and observed structure-activity relationships (SAR). Complementary AI-based structure predictions (AlphaFold3, Chai-1, and Boltz) recapitulated the energetically accessible orthosteric poses but not the dynamically stable pose selected by the MD simulations, underscoring the importance of kinetic-stability validation in antagonist pose selection. Notably, in a diet-induced obesity (DIO) mouse model, YL410 administration induced significant weight loss and exerted blood glucose-lowering effects. Collectively, this study presents the first potent, selective, and in vivo efficacious GPR15 antagonist, providing new insights into the development of therapeutics for the treatment of obesity.

title: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled RNA therapeutic design: from molecular optimization to system-level evaluation.
authors: Wang, Yongtian; Wu, Jiaqi
abstract: RNA therapeutics are increasingly moving from empirical screening towards rational, computation-guided design. Recent advances in RNA language models, generative models and structure-aware learning have improved sequence representation, candidate generation and structure-constrained optimization. However, favourable molecular properties do not necessarily translate into desirable biological performance, because therapeutic outcomes also depend on modality-specific mechanisms, delivery and exposure, molecular interactions, cellular state, immune responses and network-level adaptation. Here, we review AI-enabled RNA therapeutic design through the specific lens of the interface between molecular optimization and system-level evaluation. We compare the design constraints of siRNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, aptamers, mRNAs and translation-oriented circRNAs, and examine the capabilities and current limitations of sequence-, generative- and structure-based computational models. We further discuss the data resources and perturbation representations required to connect molecular candidates with broader cellular-response models. In this context, virtual cells are considered as approximate computational frameworks for candidate prioritization and risk-oriented system-level assessment rather than complete digital replicas of living cells. Finally, we outline a conceptual generation-simulation-feedback-optimization framework for integrating molecular design with progressively higher-level evaluation. This perspective emphasizes the need for better interfaces among RNA design, pharmacological context and cellular-response modelling, rather than relying on molecular optimization alone.

title: Molecular Recognition and Immunopharmacological Implications of Serratiopeptidase Targeting Snake Venom Bradykinin-Potentiating Peptides.
authors: Dhiman, Ankita; Singh, Rahul; Purohit, Rituraj
abstract: PURPOSE: Bradykinin-potentiating peptides (BPPs), found in snake venom, are known to modulate cardiovascular functions, but their susceptibility to enzymatic degradation remains poorly understood. METHODS: Models were generated using AlphaFold-Colab for five small BPPs (< 9 amino acids) that did not have experimentally solved structures, and those BPPs which had reliable predictions of structure (pLDDT > 80) were used for docking studies. Protein-peptide docking experiments were done using HADDOCK for studying the interaction between wild-type (WT) and mutant serratiopeptidase with BPPs. After selecting the best complex, simulation of the complex was done using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for 100 ns and binding energy determination using MM/PBSA analysis. For checking the mechanical stability of the protein-peptide complexes, Steered MD was performed. RESULTS: HADDOCK docking identified BPP-4 as a favorable binder of WT and mutant serratiopeptidase supported by a HADDOCK score of -109.1 +/- 5.2 and minimal restraint violations. MD simulations revealed greater stability in the mutant complex supported by persistent hydrogen bonds, reduced RMSD/RMSF fluctuations, restricted conformational sampling in PCA, favorable MM/PBSA energy contributions, and a more stable conformational ensemble in cluster analysis. The Steered MD simulation showed a higher rupture force in the mutant BPP-4-serratiopeptidase complex compared to the WT. CONCLUSIONS: Computational analysis identified BPP-4 as a promising serratiopeptidase-binding peptide, with differences in binding affinity and mechanical stability between WT and mutant complexes. The results offer insight into BPP-serratiopeptidase recognition at the molecular level and set the basis for future experiments on peptide binding.

title: Benchmarking Boltz-2 for relative kinase-inhibitor interaction patterns across conformational states and resistance mutations.
authors: Suenaga, Atsushi; Okimoto, Noriaki
abstract: Generative structure-prediction models can directly predict protein-ligand complexes from sequence and ligand information, but their ability to capture pharmacologically relevant kinase-inhibitor interactions remains incompletely understood. We systematically evaluated Boltz-2 using curated biochemical IC(50) measurements across eight human kinases, nine clinically used inhibitors, and representative resistance mutations. Although predicted log(10)(IC(50)) values showed a compressed dynamic range relative to experimental measurements, mutation-dependent shifts in inhibitor sensitivity, inhibitor selectivity patterns, and overall potency rankings showed substantial agreement with the experimental patterns within the present benchmark. Predicted binding probability showed good discrimination between binder and non-binder pairs within the present benchmark and a consistent inverse relationship with experimental potency. Structural analyses showed that ligand-pose variability was associated with prediction behavior within the evaluated kinase-inhibitor systems, even when kinase-domain structures showed close agreement with the corresponding experimental structures. Larger ligand RMSD values were not associated with larger prediction errors in magnitude, but were linked to systematic shifts in prediction bias, indicating that ligand-pose accuracy and predictive utility are not equivalent measures of Boltz-2 performance. These findings suggest that, within the present benchmark, relative kinase-inhibitor interaction patterns were reproduced more consistently than absolute potency values. We provide a framework for interpreting Boltz-2 outputs within the kinase-inhibitor systems examined here.

title: Bioinformatics-driven discovery of bioactive natural peptides from cyanobacterial genomes.
authors: Tabarzad, Maryam; Heidari, Mohadeseh; Norouzi, Bita
abstract: Cyanobacteria, as photosynthetic microorganisms, are emerging as a significant source of bioactive peptides with tremendous therapeutic potential against cancer, infections, and inflammatory diseases. Recent studies have highlighted that cyanobacteria produce a wide variety of non-ribosomal peptides (NRPs), polyketides (PKs), hybrids of NRPs and PKs, as well as ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs). They are produced through modular biosynthetic pathways that involve NRPS, PKS, and hybrid systems, along with extensive enzymatic modifications, resulting in large families of related compounds. The current review highlights advanced bioinformatics techniques that improve our capacity to discover and characterize natural biomaterials from cyanobacterial genomes, focusing on both ribosomally and non-ribosomally synthesized peptides. Advanced genome mining tools, such as antiSMASH and PRISM, alongside specialized databases like the Cyanobacterial Metabolomics Database (CyanoMetDB), are revolutionizing our understanding of biosynthetic gene clusters and biochemical scaffold prediction.
